body:
In Part 1 we watched Spring Data's saveAll() take 7x longer than batched persist() because every entity triggers a SELECT before its INSERT. In Part 2 we switched to raw JDBC and cut the time further. But Hibernate still sits well behind — so how close can it actually get to the bare metal?
Three settings close 80% of the gap: implement Persistable to kill the pre-INSERT SELECTs (8x faster saveAll), use StatelessSession to drop the first-level cache (35% faster persist), and layer useBulkCopyForBatchInsert=true on top (another 2–2.5x). Combined with proper batch sizing, this is as fast as Hibernate gets.
The saveAll Problem: SELECT Before INSERT When you call repository.saveAll(entities), Spring Data JPA checks each entity's ID. If the ID is non-null, it assumes the entity might already exist and calls EntityManager.merge() — which issues a SELECT before the INSERT. For 100,000 entities, that's 100,000 extra SELECTs.
Fix: Implement Persistable The fix is simple: make your entity implement Persistable<T> and always return true from isNew():
1@Entity 2@Table(name = "person") 3public class PersistablePerson implements Persistable<Integer> { 4 @Id 5 private int personId; 6 private String userName; 7 private String firstName; 8 private String lastName; 9 private int years; 10 11 @Transient 12 private boolean isNew = true; 13 14 @Override 15 public Integer getId() { return personId; } 16 17 @Override 18 public boolean isNew() { return isNew; } 19 20 @PostPersist 21 @PostLoad 22 void markNotNew() { this.isNew = false; } 23} When isNew() returns true, Spring Data uses persist() (direct INSERT) instead of merge() (SELECT + INSERT). The @PostPersist and @PostLoad callbacks reset the flag after the entity is saved or loaded from the database.
Results Strategy 100k persons (avg ms) saveAll (original, Part 1) 27,794 saveAll + Persistable 3,426 persist in chunks (Part 1) 4,048 Persistable makes saveAll 8x faster — and now slightly faster than manual persist-in-chunks! The SELECT elimination is the single biggest win.
StatelessSession: Bare-Metal Hibernate Hibernate's StatelessSession is designed for bulk operations. It bypasses:
First-level cache — no entity state tracking, constant memory Dirty checking — no scanning managed entities at flush time Cascading — related entities must be inserted explicitly 1@Repository 2public class StatelessSessionInsertRepository { 3 private final EntityManagerFactory entityManagerFactory; 4 5 public void insertStateless(List<Person> people, int batchSize) { 6 SessionFactory sf = entityManagerFactory.unwrap(SessionFactory.class); 7 8 try (StatelessSession session = sf.openStatelessSession()) { 9 session.getTransaction().begin(); 10 session.doWork(conn -> conn.createStatement().execute("SET NOCOUNT ON")); 11 12 for (int i = 0; i < people.size(); i++) { 13 session.insert(people.get(i)); 14 } 15 16 session.getTransaction().commit(); 17 } 18 } 19} Results Strategy 100k persons (avg ms) Hibernate persist (Part 1) 4,048 StatelessSession 2,650 JDBC PreparedStatement (Part 2) 2,423 JdbcTemplate (Part 2) 2,985 StatelessSession is 35% faster than regular Hibernate persist and within striking distance of raw JDBC. The remaining gap (~10%) is Hibernate's SQL generation and parameter binding overhead.
The Killer Combo: StatelessSession + useBulkCopyForBatchInsert Remember the useBulkCopyForBatchInsert=true connection string parameter from Part 4? It transparently converts PreparedStatement batches to SQL Server's Bulk Copy protocol. It works with StatelessSession too:
Strategy Normal bulkCopy=true Speedup Hibernate persist 4,048 2,144 1.9x StatelessSession 2,650 1,075 2.5x JdbcTemplate 3,089 1,373 2.3x Plain JDBC 3,953 1,516 2.6x StatelessSession + bulkCopy=true = 1,075ms — that's just 2x slower than the raw Bulk API (492ms), while still using Hibernate's mapping metadata. For applications that need ORM convenience with near-JDBC performance, this is the sweet spot.
provider_disables_autocommit The hibernate.connection.provider_disables_autocommit setting tells Hibernate that the connection pool already disabled auto-commit, skipping the setAutoCommit(false) JDBC round-trip per transaction. To use it, you need both:
1spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.connection.provider_disables_autocommit=true 2spring.datasource.hikari.auto-commit=false Strategy Normal +noAutoCommit Speedup Hibernate persist 4,048 4,094 None Persistable saveAll 3,426 2,956 14% Verdict: negligible for persist, modest for saveAll. The saved round-trip is only measurable when there are many small transactions (saveAll with frequent flushes) rather than one large batch (persist). Not worth the configuration complexity unless you have a very specific transactional pattern.
Batch Size Sweet Spot Parts 1-4 tested batch sizes of 10, 100, 1000, and 5000. A fine-grained sweep (50-2000 in steps of 50) reveals the actual inflection points:
Bulk API Batch Avg ms Batch Avg ms 50 4,565 600 834 100 3,119 800 1,194 200 1,874 1000 1,099 400 1,196 1400 675 500 980 2000 618 Bulk API: diminishing returns past 500. The sweet spot is 500-2000 with wide variance (single-run noise). Use 1000 as a safe default.
JdbcTemplate Batch Avg ms Batch Avg ms 50 6,471 600 2,989 100 6,036 700 2,847 200 5,291 800 2,975 500 3,062 1600 2,996 JdbcTemplate: optimal at 700, with minimal improvement past 500. Larger batches (1000+) don't help because the driver's TCP buffer and SQL Server's batch processing saturate around 500-800 rows.
Multi-Value Sweet Spot Part 3 showed that multi-value INSERT (objectsPerInsert > 1) is much faster than single-row inserts. But what's the optimal value? A fine-grained sweep reveals:
objectsPerInsert Avg ms vs single-row 1 3,984 — 10 1,711 2.3x faster 50 1,038 3.8x 100 983 4.1x 200 828 4.8x fastest 300 1,033 3.9x 400 1,360 2.9x Optimal: 200 values per INSERT. After 200, SQL Server's query parser overhead for the growing SQL string outweighs the network round-trip savings. The sweet spot is 100-200 — enough to amortize per-statement overhead without overwhelming the parser.
Remember: SQL Server's maximum parameter count is 2,100. With 5 columns per row, objectsPerInsert cannot exceed 420 (2100/5 = 420).
Connection String: sendStringParametersAsUnicode Setting sendStringParametersAsUnicode=false in the JDBC URL tells the driver to send string parameters as VARCHAR instead of NVARCHAR. This can help when your table has VARCHAR columns (avoids implicit conversion), but has no effect on NVARCHAR columns:
Strategy Unicode (default) sendStringParametersAsUnicode=false Bulk API 691ms 812ms (no improvement) JdbcTemplate 3,699ms 3,892ms (no improvement) If your columns are NVARCHAR, skip this setting.
Transaction Patterns How you structure transactions matters more than how big they are:
Pattern 100k rows (avg ms) Notes One large transaction (commit at end) 3,773 Baseline Commit per batch (every 1000 rows) 3,543 Marginally faster Savepoints per batch 3,949 Slightly slower (overhead) Auto-commit per row (10k rows only) 5,198 ms for 10k rows (~52,000ms extrapolated) 15x slower Verdict: auto-commit per row is catastrophic — each INSERT becomes its own transaction with its own log flush. Any explicit transaction (batched or whole-run) is dramatically faster. The difference between commit-per-batch and commit-at-end is noise.
Isolation Levels Isolation 100k rows (avg ms) READ_UNCOMMITTED 3,189 READ_COMMITTED (default) 3,037 SERIALIZABLE 2,963 Isolation level has no measurable impact on INSERT-only workloads. The isolation level primarily affects reads and locking behavior — there's nothing for an INSERT to "read dirtily" or "serialize against". Don't bother tuning isolation level for bulk-load performance.
GC and JVM Memory Tuning Does the Java garbage collector affect database insert throughput? We ran the same test with four GC/heap configurations:
GC Heap Bulk API (ms) JdbcTemplate (ms) Total GC pause G1 (default) 512 MB 687 3,194 ~59-138 ms G1 4 GB 762 3,095 ~93-139 ms Parallel 2 GB 863 3,401 ~21-59 ms ZGC 4 GB 867 3,291 ~109-315 ms GC choice has essentially no impact on insert performance for this workload. The reasons:
Short-lived objects fit in young generation — Person instances die quickly after being batched and sent to the driver. All GCs handle this well. GC pauses are tiny compared to database I/O (300ms of GC vs 30+ seconds of total time). ZGC has slight overhead — its concurrent collection isn't needed when heap pressure is low. Takeaway: stick with the default G1 and modest heap size (512 MB-1 GB is enough for 100k-row batches). Over-tuning the JVM for database workloads is a waste of time — the bottleneck is the network/disk, not Java.
The one thing to remember StatelessSession + useBulkCopyForBatchInsert=true = 1,075 ms for 100k inserts — 2x slower than raw Bulk Copy (492 ms), with ORM mapping metadata still working for you. If you need Hibernate's convenience without paying Hibernate's full price, that's the combination.
If you can only make one change to speed up a saveAll() call: implement Persistable<T> with isNew = true. It eliminates the pre-INSERT SELECTs and makes saveAll 8x faster — a 10-line code change for a 10x result.
Test yourself Which Hibernate features help close the gap to raw JDBC? (select all that apply)
StatelessSession Implementing Persistable with isNew=true useBulkCopyForBatchInsert=true Second-level cache Check answer StatelessSession, Persistable (isNew=true) and useBulkCopyForBatchInsert together close about 80% of the gap. The second-level cache is a read optimization and does not help inserts.
Next: Part 6 — Parallel Inserts splits the data across multiple connections to see how far parallel threads can push it.
title: Fastest MS SQL Inserts — Part 5: Hibernate Tuning

body:
Every strategy we've tested so far — Hibernate, JDBC, Bulk API — pushes data through a single connection. SQL Server handles concurrent writes just fine; the bottleneck is the serial nature of one TCP stream. Split 100k rows across 4 threads with 4 connections and the Bulk API drops from 492 ms to 330 ms, the fastest Java-client result in the whole series.
But parallelism isn't a free lunch — threads past 4 give diminishing returns, concurrent readers slow the writers 2.5x, and the TABLOCK hint changes the trade-off. Here's where the inflection points actually are.
The Approach The idea is straightforward:
Partition the data into N chunks (one per thread) Each thread opens its own connection from the HikariCP pool Each thread inserts its chunk independently Wait for all threads to complete 1@Service 2public class ParallelInsertExecutor { 3 private final BulkCopyRepository bulkCopyRepository; 4 5 public void parallelBulkApiInsert(List<Person> people, 6 TableDescriptor<Person> table, 7 int batchSize, int threadCount) { 8 List<List<Person>> chunks = partition(people, threadCount); 9 ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threadCount); 10 11 List<CompletableFuture<Void>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); 12 for (List<Person> chunk : chunks) { 13 futures.add(CompletableFuture.runAsync( 14 () -> bulkCopyRepository.performBulkInsert(chunk, table, batchSize), 15 executor)); 16 } 17 CompletableFuture.allOf(futures.toArray(new CompletableFuture[0])).join(); 18 executor.shutdown(); 19 } 20} Important: HikariCP's pool size must be at least threadCount, otherwise threads block waiting for connections. The default pool size (10) is fine for up to 10 threads.
Thread Count Sweep: Bulk API Threads Avg ms Speedup vs 1 thread 1 1,155 1.0x 2 998 1.2x 4 537 2.2x 8 434 2.7x 16 442 2.6x 4 threads is the sweet spot for Bulk API. Going to 8 threads helps slightly, but 16 threads is actually marginally slower — the SQL Server bulk copy engine saturates the I/O subsystem and additional threads just add contention.
Thread Count Sweep: JdbcTemplate Threads Avg ms Speedup vs 1 thread 1 4,048 1.0x 2 3,292 1.2x 4 2,407 1.7x 8 1,937 2.1x 16 608 6.7x JdbcTemplate benefits much more from parallelism — because each thread's PreparedStatement batch is independent and the driver sends SQL statements over TCP. More threads = more concurrent TCP streams = more bandwidth utilization. The 16-thread result (608ms) is remarkable.
The Ultimate Combination: Multi-Value + Parallel What happens when we combine multi-value inserts (400 values per INSERT, from Part 3) with parallel threads?
Strategy Avg ms Multi-value 400, 1 thread 1,058 Multi-value 400, 4 threads 426 Multi-value 400, 8 threads 368 Parallel Bulk API, 4 threads 330 Multi-value 400 + 8 threads (368ms) is competitive with parallel Bulk API (330ms) — and the multi-value approach works with any JDBC driver, not just MS SQL Server's Bulk API.
Important caveat: Multi-value INSERT is incompatible with useBulkCopyForBatchInsert=true (see Part 8 for details). You must choose one or the other — both are excellent, but they cannot be combined.
Scaling to 1 Million Rows Strategy 100k rows 1M rows Scales linearly? Bulk API (single) 492 6,225 ~12.7x (yes) Parallel Bulk API 4t 330 4,427 ~13.4x (yes) TVP 818 7,314 ~8.9x (yes) JdbcTemplate 2,985 11,914 ~4x (sublinear!) All strategies scale roughly linearly with data size. JdbcTemplate actually gets better at scale because the fixed overhead (connection setup, batch compilation) is amortized over more rows.
Practical Considerations Connection pool sizing: Set spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size to at least your thread count. Setting it too high wastes SQL Server connections.
ID generation: If using application-generated IDs, ensure no collisions across threads. In our test, each thread gets a distinct partition so IDs don't overlap.
Error handling: If one thread fails, the others may have already committed. Use a CountDownLatch or check futures for exceptions before declaring success.
Lock contention: SQL Server uses row-level locking for INSERTs by default. You won't get table locks unless you're inserting into the same page from many threads simultaneously with very small rows.
Concurrent Reads During Insert In production, tables aren't idle during bulk loads — other sessions are reading. How much does concurrent reading impact insert performance?
Scenario Bulk API (avg ms) No concurrent reads 814 4 reader threads (SELECT COUNT/AVG) 2,037 (2.5x slower) Concurrent readers slow inserts by 2.5x, even when readers use WITH (NOLOCK). The slowdown comes from I/O contention and SQL Server's latch management on the data pages being written.
TABLOCK hint can help here — it acquires a table-level lock that prevents readers entirely, allowing uninterrupted bulk insertion:
Hint JDBC batch (avg ms) No hint (row locks) 4,240 WITH (TABLOCK) 2,991 (30% faster) Trade-off: TABLOCK blocks all other writers AND readers during the insert. Use it only for dedicated bulk load windows.
The one thing to remember 4 threads × Bulk API = 330 ms. You can't go meaningfully faster from a Java client. 8 threads saves another 100 ms; 16 threads is noise. Multi-value INSERT at 400 rows per statement × 8 threads gets 368 ms without needing the Bulk API at all.
If your load window overlaps with concurrent SELECTs, parallel inserts take ~2.5x longer. Use WITH (TABLOCK) for dedicated windows — otherwise, pick 4 threads and move on.
Test yourself How many threads is the sweet spot for Parallel Bulk API inserts?
1-2 threads 4-8 threads 16 threads One thread per row Check answer 4 threads hit 330 ms; 8 threads shaved another ~100 ms; 16 threads was noise. 4-8 is the practical sweet spot.
Next: Part 7 — Index Impact measures the hidden cost of non-clustered indexes during bulk loads.
title: Fastest MS SQL Inserts — Part 6: Parallel Threads

body:
Every production table has indexes. Every INSERT has to maintain them. Add 5 non-clustered indexes to a table and the Bulk API — the fastest single-thread strategy — slows down 7x. The other strategies converge: with enough indexes, the choice of insert strategy stops mattering because index maintenance dominates.
But that's only the start. The surrounding table design decisions matter as much: row width, compression, columnstore, fill factor, GUID vs INT keys, change tracking, temporal history, JSON/XML indexes, statistics auto-update, encryption, and so on all impose their own INSERT tax — and some of them are counter-intuitive (compression makes inserts slower; stats OFF makes them slower; sparse columns are worse than nothing when filled).
This post measures them all. If you only read the first table, index count is the headline — but the rest of the post is where the surprises live.
The Test We create 0, 1, 3, or 5 non-clustered indexes on the person table, then run the same 100,000-row insert with three strategies: Bulk API, JdbcTemplate, and Hibernate persist.
1@Service 2public class IndexBenchmarkHelper { 3 private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate; 4 5 // Five indexes representing realistic patterns 6 private static final List<IndexDef> ALL_INDEXES = Arrays.asList( 7 new IndexDef("IX_person_username", "person", "user_name"), 8 new IndexDef("IX_person_lastname", "person", "last_name"), 9 new IndexDef("IX_person_firstname", "person", "first_name"), 10 new IndexDef("IX_person_years", "person", "years"), 11 new IndexDef("IX_person_name_composite", "person", "last_name, first_name") 12 ); 13 14 public void setIndexCount(int count) { 15 dropAllIndexes(); 16 for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) { 17 createIndex(ALL_INDEXES.get(i)); 18 } 19 } 20} The indexes represent a mix of:
Selective columns (username — unique values) Low-selectivity columns (years — few distinct values) Composite indexes (last_name + first_name) Results Bulk API Indexes Avg ms Slowdown vs 0 0 784 — 1 1,829 +133% 3 3,632 +363% 5 5,290 +575% JdbcTemplate Indexes Avg ms Slowdown vs 0 0 4,572 — 1 5,672 +24% 3 6,614 +45% 5 10,330 +126% Hibernate Persist Indexes Avg ms Slowdown vs 0 0 3,209 — 1 4,676 +46% 3 7,563 +136% 5 8,564 +167% Analysis Bulk API is the most sensitive With 0 indexes, Bulk API is by far the fastest (784ms). But with 5 indexes, it's 5,290ms — slower than JdbcTemplate with 0 indexes. The reason: Bulk API uses minimal-logging INSERT operations that bypass some of the normal logging overhead. But when non-clustered indexes exist, the engine must update each index B-tree for every row, and this overhead dominates.
JdbcTemplate is the most resilient JdbcTemplate's index penalty is relatively modest: only 2.3x slower with 5 indexes vs 0. Since JdbcTemplate sends standard INSERT statements, the SQL Server optimizer can plan the index maintenance more efficiently.
The crossover point With 3+ indexes, all strategies converge to similar performance. The strategy choice matters less when index maintenance dominates the insert cost.
Practical Implications Drop indexes before bulk loads if possible. Recreating them after is often faster than maintaining them during the insert.
Choose your strategy based on your table's index count:
0-1 indexes: Bulk API is king 3+ indexes: JdbcTemplate or Hibernate — the overhead is comparable Many indexes: Consider ALTER INDEX ... DISABLE before load, then rebuild Composite indexes cost the same as single-column indexes for insert overhead. A composite index on (last_name, first_name) costs the same as two separate single-column indexes.
Filtered indexes (with a WHERE clause) are cheaper — they only need updating when the inserted row matches the filter.
Index count: the summary Indexes Fastest strategy Avg ms Slowdown vs 0 0 Bulk API 784 — 1 Bulk API 1,829 2.3x 3 ~Any (converges) 7,563 10x 5 ~Any (converges) 8,564 11x A table with 5 non-clustered indexes is 6-11x slower to load than one with just the clustered PK — and the choice of insert strategy barely matters anymore. The actionable advice: disable non-essential indexes before bulk loads, rebuild them after.
Beyond Indexes: Table Design & Logging Choices The index count is only one dimension of INSERT cost. Below are 10 more table-design decisions that each add their own tax, in order of magnitude:
Row size impact Wider rows = proportionally slower inserts, regardless of strategy:
Row Type Columns ~Row Size 100k rows (avg ms) Narrow (person) 5 ~60 bytes 3,699 Wide (20 cols) 17 ~1.5 KB 6,952 (1.9x slower) LOB (NVARCHAR(MAX)) 7 ~3 KB 9,834 (2.7x slower per row, 50k rows) LOB columns (NVARCHAR(MAX)) force row-overflow storage and out-of-row allocation, adding significant I/O overhead beyond the raw data size increase.
Data compression SQL Server supports ROW and PAGE compression on tables:
Compression 100k rows (avg ms) vs None None 2,417 — ROW 2,595 +7% slower PAGE 3,229 +33% slower Compression makes inserts slower, not faster. The CPU overhead of compressing each row or page outweighs any I/O savings. For narrow rows like our person table, compression adds cost without meaningful space savings. Compression is a read optimization (smaller pages = faster scans), not a write optimization.
Columnstore index Columnstore indexes store data in compressed column segments rather than row pages. They excel at analytical queries but have different insert characteristics:
Table Type Batch Size 100k rows (avg ms) B-tree (clustered PK) 1,000 2,417 Columnstore 1,000 8,402 (3.5x slower) Columnstore 5,000 4,880 (2x slower) Columnstore inserts are slower because data goes into a delta store (a hidden B-tree rowgroup) until it reaches ~1 million rows, then gets compressed into a columnstore segment. Larger batch sizes help because they fill the delta store faster, triggering compression sooner.
Heap + TABLOCK (minimal logging) A heap table (no clustered index) with the TABLOCK hint enables minimal logging in SIMPLE/BULK_LOGGED recovery mode:
Table Hint 100k rows (avg ms) Clustered PK (person) None 2,401 Clustered PK (person) TABLOCK 2,185 (9% faster) Heap (no PK) None 4,073 Heap (no PK) TABLOCK 2,579 (37% faster) The heap without TABLOCK is surprisingly slow — without a clustered index, SQL Server uses IAM-driven allocation which leads to page contention. TABLOCK fixes this by allowing bulk allocation. But a clustered table with TABLOCK is still fastest overall.
BCP (bcp.exe) — the external baseline The bcp command-line utility is SQL Server's native bulk loader:
1bcp testdb.dbo.person in data.txt -c -t"\t" -S localhost,1433 -U weblogic -P weblogic -b 1000 Method 100k rows (avg ms) BCP utility 843 Java Bulk API 691 Java parallel Bulk API 4t 330 BCP (843ms) is slower than the Java Bulk API (691ms). This is because BCP reads from a flat file (disk I/O) while our Java tests generate data in memory. BCP also does not parallelize across connections. The Java Bulk API over in-memory data is the actual performance ceiling.
Fill factor tuning The clustered index fill factor controls how full each page is filled during index creation/rebuild. Lower fill factor = more empty space per page = fewer page splits during random-key inserts, at the cost of more pages (larger table size, more I/O on reads).
Fill Factor Bulk API (avg ms) JdbcTemplate (avg ms) 50 1,762 5,377 70 1,199 4,252 90 869 3,395 100 (default) 916 3,337 Fill factor 100 is fastest for sequential inserts — which makes sense: our test inserts monotonically increasing IDs, so there are no page splits regardless of fill factor. Lower fill factors just waste space. Lower fill factors (70-80) help when you have random-key inserts or heavy update patterns that cause page splits.
Partitioning & SWITCH SQL Server partitioning splits a table into independent chunks on-disk. The SWITCH PARTITION command atomically swaps a staging table into a partition — a metadata-only operation that takes milliseconds regardless of row count:
1-- Partition function and scheme 2CREATE PARTITION FUNCTION pf_person(INT) AS RANGE LEFT FOR VALUES (25000, 50000, 75000); 3CREATE PARTITION SCHEME ps_person AS PARTITION pf_person ALL TO ([PRIMARY]); 4 5-- SWITCH operation (metadata-only, no data movement) 6ALTER TABLE person_staging SWITCH TO person_partitioned PARTITION 4; Method 100k rows (avg ms) Direct insert into partitioned table 4,652 SWITCH pattern (bulk-load heap, then SWITCH) 3,470 (25% faster) The SWITCH pattern is faster because the heavy work (bulk loading) happens on an unpartitioned heap table, and only the final metadata update touches the partitioned table. This is the industry standard for zero-downtime bulk loads — the main table stays queryable throughout the load.
Caveat: The staging table must have an identical schema plus a CHECK constraint matching the target partition's range. Both tables must live on the same filegroup.
Clustered key: INT vs GUID The clustered key defines the physical order of rows on disk. Random keys (like UUIDs) cause page splits — new rows must be inserted into the middle of existing pages, so SQL Server has to split a full page in two and copy half the rows.
Clustered Key 100k rows (avg ms) Notes INT sequential (baseline) 3,015 No page splits GUID sequential (NEWSEQUENTIALID()) 3,340 (+11%) Monotonic — no page splits GUID random (UUID.randomUUID()) 3,588 (+19%) Page splits all over the index The 19% penalty for random GUIDs is actually small — because we inserted into an empty table. On an existing populated table, random GUIDs can be 2-5x slower as the index grows and new insertions hit densely-packed pages. If you must use GUIDs, prefer NEWSEQUENTIALID() on SQL Server or an "ordered GUID" (UUIDv7/ULID) on the application side.
Change Tracking SQL Server Change Tracking is a lightweight CDC alternative that records which rows were modified (not the changed values). It's enabled per-database and per-table:
1ALTER DATABASE testdb SET CHANGE_TRACKING = ON (CHANGE_RETENTION = 2 DAYS, AUTO_CLEANUP = ON); 2ALTER TABLE person_ct ENABLE CHANGE_TRACKING WITH (TRACK_COLUMNS_UPDATED = OFF); Scenario 100k rows (avg ms) No change tracking 3,206 Change Tracking enabled 5,205 (62% slower) Change Tracking has significant insert overhead — each row generates an internal side-table entry with the operation and version. Enable it only if downstream consumers actually need the change feed. For audit alone, temporal tables are cheaper.
Note: Full Change Data Capture (CDC) — which records entire row values — is Enterprise-only and would have even higher overhead than CT.
Temporal (system-versioned) tables Temporal tables automatically track row history in a shadow table. Every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE writes to both the current table and the history table:
1CREATE TABLE person_temporal ( 2 person_id INT PRIMARY KEY, 3 user_name NVARCHAR(30), first_name NVARCHAR(10), 4 last_name NVARCHAR(15), years INT, 5 ValidFrom DATETIME2 GENERATED ALWAYS AS ROW START NOT NULL, 6 ValidTo DATETIME2 GENERATED ALWAYS AS ROW END NOT NULL, 7 PERIOD FOR SYSTEM_TIME (ValidFrom, ValidTo) 8) WITH (SYSTEM_VERSIONING = ON); Scenario 100k rows (avg ms) Plain table 3,009 Temporal table (SYSTEM_VERSIONED) 3,936 (+31%) Surprisingly cheap — only 31% overhead for full point-in-time history. Compare that to the AFTER INSERT trigger approach from Part 8 which was 2.2x slower. For audit requirements, temporal tables are the right answer.
For pure inserts the history table doesn't receive rows (only updates/deletes populate it), so the overhead is almost entirely the extra period column maintenance.
Filtered & INCLUDE indexes Not all non-clustered indexes are created equal. Two variations can dramatically cut insert cost:
Filtered index — only indexes rows matching a WHERE clause (WHERE years >= 50) INCLUDE index — stores extra columns only at the leaf level (not in the sort key) Index Type 100k rows (avg ms) vs no index No index (baseline) 2,782 — Filtered (only ~17% of rows match) 3,461 +24% INCLUDE 3,824 +37% Composite 3-column 4,071 +46% Full non-clustered 4,956 +78% Filtered indexes are the biggest win: 60% cheaper than a full index on the same column because most rows never touch the index. If your queries only need "the senior customers", only index them.
INCLUDE beats composite by 30% because INCLUDE columns aren't maintained in sort order — they're just stored at the leaf level for covering reads.
Computed columns Computed columns are either PERSISTED (materialized on write) or non-persisted (computed on read).
1CREATE TABLE person_computed ( 2 person_id INT PRIMARY KEY, user_name NVARCHAR(30), first_name NVARCHAR(10), 3 last_name NVARCHAR(15), years INT, 4 full_name AS (first_name + N' ' + last_name) PERSISTED, 5 years_bucket AS (CASE WHEN years < 30 THEN N'young' ELSE N'old' END) 6) Scenario 100k rows (avg ms) Plain table 2,782 Table with 1 persisted + 1 non-persisted computed column 2,707 Essentially free. The persisted column's string concatenation adds negligible CPU cost compared to I/O. The non-persisted column costs nothing on insert — it's evaluated on reads. Use them freely for derived values; they're much cleaner than application-side computations and support indexing.
Trace flag 610 TF 610 is a legacy trace flag that enables minimally-logged bulk inserts into clustered tables.
Setting 100k rows (avg ms) TF 610 OFF + TABLOCK 2,336 TF 610 ON + TABLOCK 2,386 No measurable difference for our workload. Why? TF 610 helps BULK INSERT, INSERT INTO ... SELECT, and BCP operations — not regular INSERT statements with addBatch(). The MS SQL JDBC driver's Bulk Copy API already uses minimal logging when applicable. Skip this flag unless you're using BULK INSERT or BCP directly.
Delayed durability DELAYED_DURABILITY = FORCED makes transaction commits asynchronous — the log flush happens on a background timer instead of synchronously at COMMIT. Risk: a crash loses recent transactions.
Setting 100k rows (avg ms) DISABLED (default) 3,147 FORCED 4,698 (49% SLOWER!) Counter-intuitive finding. Delayed durability makes our test slower, not faster. Why?
Delayed durability batches multiple small transactions' log flushes together. It helps workloads with many frequent small COMMITs (think OLTP with per-row inserts). Our test uses one large transaction, so there's nothing to batch — DD just adds coordination overhead without any benefit.
Takeaway: DD is a per-transaction optimization. For bulk inserts, use fewer, larger transactions instead of enabling DD on frequent small ones.
XML vs JSON columns Semi-structured data in SQL Server comes in two flavors:
XML column type: Schema-less XML with built-in XQuery support, validation on insert JSON stored as NVARCHAR(MAX) + CHECK (ISJSON(data) = 1): Lightweight JSON validation Column Type 100k rows (avg ms) vs baseline JSON (NVARCHAR + ISJSON check) 4,752 +60% XML column 10,916 +270% XML is 2.3x slower than JSON for the same semantic payload. XML columns:
Parse the XML into a native tree representation on insert Validate well-formedness Store in an optimized binary tree format (not the original string) If you need semi-structured storage, prefer JSON (NVARCHAR + ISJSON) unless you specifically need XQuery, XPath or XML schema validation.
Sparse columns Sparse columns are SQL Server's optimization for tables with many mostly-NULL columns:
Column type / fill pattern 100k rows (avg ms) Non-sparse, mostly NULL 3,912 Sparse, mostly NULL 4,005 (+2% — essentially tied) Non-sparse, mostly filled 5,053 Sparse, mostly filled 5,772 (+14% slower!) Surprise: sparse columns offer no insert benefit when NULL-heavy (expected tie) but are 14% SLOWER when filled. Sparse columns use a special on-disk representation that's efficient for NULL storage but more expensive when the column has a value. Use SPARSE only when:
The column is >95% NULL on real data You're optimizing storage (sparse saves disk space) rather than insert speed AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS 1ALTER DATABASE testdb SET AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS { ON | OFF } Setting 100k rows (avg ms) AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS = ON (default) 2,966 AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS = OFF 4,474 (50% SLOWER!) Counter-intuitive: turning OFF auto-stats doesn't speed up inserts — it slows the overall workload by 50%. Why? With stats OFF, SQL Server's query optimizer makes poor decisions for the INSERT plan itself. The optimizer uses statistics to choose index access paths, batch sizes, and memory grants even for simple INSERTs with no WHERE clause.
Takeaway: leave AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS on. The savings from skipping stats maintenance are dwarfed by the cost of a worse query plan.
Server-side encryption (ENCRYPTBYPASSPHRASE) SQL Server supports server-side encryption via ENCRYPTBYKEY, ENCRYPTBYPASSPHRASE, etc. We tested with 3 encrypted columns per row (user_name, first_name, last_name):
Scenario 100k rows (avg ms) Plain insert 3,948 3 columns ENCRYPTBYPASSPHRASE 15,952 (4x slower) Encryption is CPU-expensive. The actual AES-256 operations happen server-side, consuming SQL Server CPU. Minimize the number of encrypted columns and consider:
Always Encrypted — client-side encryption (CPU cost moves to the app) TDE — database-level encryption (works at page level, lower per-row overhead) Column-level encryption only on actual PII, not every text field ID Generation Strategies How you generate primary keys matters more than you might think:
Strategy 100k rows (avg ms) vs app-generated App-generated INT (baseline) 3,085 — IDENTITY column 3,459 +12% SET IDENTITY_INSERT ON (explicit values) 3,857 +25% SEQUENCE object (DEFAULT) 4,052 +31% IDENTITY + RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS 4,142 +34% App-side ID generation wins. The surprises:
RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS is a significant tax (+34%) — many ORMs set it by default so they can populate the entity's id field. If you don't need the generated IDs back, suppress it. SET IDENTITY_INSERT ON costs more than you'd expect — the mode toggle isn't free, and the engine has to validate uniqueness against the identity seed. SEQUENCE objects are convenient but add a DEFAULT lookup per row. Recommendation: generate IDs on the application side (ULID, Snowflake, pre-fetched sequence batch, or a SELECT NEXT VALUE FOR seq FROM GENERATE_SERIES(1,1000) pre-fetch pattern) for the fastest batched inserts.
Foreign Keys Scenario 100k rows (avg ms) No FK constraint at all 2,957 FK disabled (NOCHECK CONSTRAINT) 3,108 (+5%) FK trusted (WITH CHECK CHECK CONSTRAINT) 3,592 (+21%) Trusted (enforced) foreign keys cost about 21% — the engine validates every row's dept_id against the department table. Disabled FKs still cost a small 5% because the optimizer treats them as untrusted and may generate different plans.
For large bulk loads with known-good data: disable FK constraints, load, then re-enable with WITH CHECK to re-validate. The re-validation is faster than per-row checking.
Batch Retry Patterns Real-world data often has bad rows. How you handle one bad row in a batch has dramatic cost:
Pattern 10k rows, 1 duplicate (avg ms) Abort batch on error (clearBatch, continue) 302 Insert per-row (catch, skip, continue) 2,250 (7.5x slower) The abort-on-error pattern completes in 302ms because each 1,000-row sub-batch that contains a bad row is simply discarded (we lose up to 999 good rows per bad row). The per-row pattern inserts 9,999 of 10,000 rows but takes 7.5x longer.
The right answer depends on your data integrity requirements:
Known-good data: use the batch pattern — if any row fails, there's a bug upstream. Dirty data with some bad rows: use smaller batches (100 instead of 1000) so you lose less on each failure; the per-row path should be reserved for the final retry pass. Zero tolerance for data loss: stage into a temp table, VALIDATE then move to the real table. Temp table staging A common ETL pattern: INSERT into a heap temp table, then INSERT-SELECT into the real table:
Method 100k rows (avg ms) Direct insert 2,401 Temp table staging 4,822 (2x slower) Staging is slower for simple inserts because you're writing data twice. It's useful when you need to validate, deduplicate, or transform data before loading — not for raw throughput.
The one thing to remember Table design dominates insert speed once you have more than one non-clustered index. Five indexes slows inserts 6-11x — far more than any client-side strategy change can recover. If your bulk load is slow, drop indexes first, retry; then look at the client.
Most other table-design knobs save or cost 20-50% each. The exceptions worth remembering: server-side encryption (4x slower), XML columns (2.3x slower than JSON), AFTER INSERT triggers (2.2x slower), and AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS = OFF (50% slower — don't turn it off).
Test yourself Which settings should you leave at their defaults for fast inserts? (select all that apply)
AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS (ON) MAXDOP Fill factor (100) The number of non-clustered indexes during the load Check answer Leave AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS on, MAXDOP and fill factor at defaults. Non-clustered indexes are the thing to drop before a bulk load: 5 of them slow inserts 6-11x.
Does ROW compression make inserts faster?
Yes, less data to write No, it adds about 7% overhead Only with columnstore It has no measurable effect Check answer Compression is a read-side optimization. ROW adds about 7% and PAGE about 33% overhead on inserts because the engine compresses on write.
Next: Part 8 — TVP and Plain JDBC covers Table-Valued Parameters, bare-metal JDBC, and the final rankings across all 110+ configurations.
title: Fastest MS SQL Inserts — Part 7: Index Impact

body:
Executive Summary This series benchmarks 110+ insert strategies and tuning knobs on SQL Server 2025 Express (Windows, Java 17, Spring Boot 3.3) over 4,222 individual benchmark runs. Here's the TL;DR:
The 10 highest-impact decisions (in order) # Choice Impact 1 Batch your inserts (any strategy ≫ auto-commit per row) 15x 2 Use the Bulk Copy API (SQLServerBulkCopy / insertBulk...) 5-6x vs plain JDBC 3 Parallelize across 4 connections 2-3x on top of #2 4 Enable useBulkCopyForBatchInsert=true in the JDBC URL 2-2.5x 5 Use multi-value INSERT (200 values/statement) 4-5x for JDBC 6 Drop/disable non-essential indexes before bulk loads up to 7x 7 Pick the right batch size (500-1000) — not 10, not 10,000 4-5x vs tiny batches 8 Add WITH (TABLOCK) hint for dedicated bulk-load windows 1.3x 9 Use Persistable + isNew=true if you must use Spring Data saveAll 8x 10 Keep AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS = ON (don't try to be clever) 1.5x Top 7 counter-intuitive findings OPTION (RECOMPILE) makes batched inserts 52x slower (2.4 minutes vs 3 seconds). Delayed Durability = FORCED makes bulk inserts 49% SLOWER, not faster. It helps many-small-commits workloads, not single-large-transaction bulk loads. Natively compiled stored procs are 21x slower when called from Java per-row via addBatch. Their design assumes the C#/.NET memory-table API. In-Memory OLTP tables don't help batched Java inserts. They shine for concurrency, not batch throughput. ROW/PAGE compression make inserts slower (+7%/+33%). Compression is a read optimization. BCP utility is slower than Java Bulk API when data is in-memory. The file I/O overhead dominates. AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS = OFF makes inserts 50% SLOWER, not faster. The optimizer needs stats even for simple INSERTs. The absolute fastest paths (if your scenario allows) If your source data is already in SQL Server (ETL within the same database):
INSERT INTO target SELECT ... FROM source = 319 ms (the ultimate server-side copy) If data must come from Java:
Parallel Bulk API 4 threads = 330 ms (the standalone Java winner) The ranking The fastest I could get 100,000 person rows into SQL Server from a Java application is 330 ms (Parallel Bulk API, 4 threads). The slowest is 27,794 ms (Spring Data saveAll without Persistable) — 84x slower. Everything in between is covered in this series.
TVP (818 ms) is the best choice when you need portability across different clients and don't have SQLServerBulkCopy available. Plain JDBC (3,905 ms) is only 3% faster than Hibernate persist() — the ORM is not your bottleneck.
The rest of this post walks through every topic in the summary above, starting with two approaches that bypass Hibernate entirely: Table-Valued Parameters and plain JDBC. After that come the advanced topics — isolation, procs, plans, latency, snapshot concurrency, index trade-offs, and the full ranking across 110+ configurations.
Table-Valued Parameters (TVPs) TVPs let you send an entire table of data as a single stored procedure or query parameter. Instead of sending N individual INSERT statements, you send one request containing all the data.
Setup: Create the Table Type First, create a user-defined table type in SQL Server:
1CREATE TYPE dbo.PersonTableType AS TABLE ( 2 person_id INT, 3 user_name NVARCHAR(30), 4 first_name NVARCHAR(10), 5 last_name NVARCHAR(15), 6 years INT 7); Java Implementation The MS SQL JDBC driver provides SQLServerDataTable for building TVP data:
1@Repository 2public class TvpInsertRepository { 3 private final DataSource dataSource; 4 5 public void insertWithTvp(List<Person> people, int batchSize) { 6 String sql = "INSERT INTO person (person_id, user_name, first_name, last_name, years) " + 7 "SELECT person_id, user_name, first_name, last_name, years FROM ?"; 8 9 try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection()) { 10 conn.setAutoCommit(false); 11 12 try (CallableStatement stmt = conn.prepareCall(sql)) { 13 for (int i = 0; i < people.size(); i += batchSize) { 14 int end = Math.min(i + batchSize, people.size()); 15 SQLServerDataTable dataTable = buildDataTable(people.subList(i, end)); 16 stmt.setObject(1, dataTable); 17 stmt.execute(); 18 } 19 conn.commit(); 20 } 21 } 22 } 23 24 private SQLServerDataTable buildDataTable(List<Person> people) throws SQLException { 25 SQLServerDataTable dt = new SQLServerDataTable(); 26 dt.setTvpName("PersonTableType"); 27 dt.addColumnMetadata("person_id", Types.INTEGER); 28 dt.addColumnMetadata("user_name", Types.NVARCHAR); 29 dt.addColumnMetadata("first_name", Types.NVARCHAR); 30 dt.addColumnMetadata("last_name", Types.NVARCHAR); 31 dt.addColumnMetadata("years", Types.INTEGER); 32 33 for (Person p : people) { 34 dt.addRow(p.getPersonId(), p.getUserName(), 35 p.getFirstName(), p.getLastName(), p.getYears()); 36 } 37 return dt; 38 } 39} TVP Advantages Single round-trip per batch — the entire data table is sent as one TDS packet No 2,100-parameter limit — unlike multi-value INSERT which hits SQL Server's max param count Type-safe — SQL Server validates the table type schema Works inside transactions — unlike BULK INSERT from a file TVP Results Batch Size Avg ms 10 20,221 100 2,993 1,000 1,203 5,000 818 TVP at batch=5000 (818ms) is the 3rd fastest single-thread strategy — faster than all JDBC/Hibernate approaches, slower only than Bulk API. It's a solid middle ground.
Plain JDBC: The Bare-Metal Baseline How much overhead does Hibernate/JPA actually add? Let's find out with raw JDBC:
1@Repository 2public class PlainJdbcInsertRepository { 3 private final DataSource dataSource; 4 private static final String INSERT_SQL = 5 "INSERT INTO person (person_id, user_name, first_name, last_name, years) " + 6 "VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)"; 7 8 public void insertBatch(List<Person> people, int batchSize) { 9 try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection()) { 10 conn.setAutoCommit(false); 11 try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(INSERT_SQL)) { 12 int count = 0; 13 for (Person p : people) { 14 ps.setInt(1, p.getPersonId()); 15 ps.setString(2, p.getUserName()); 16 ps.setString(3, p.getFirstName()); 17 ps.setString(4, p.getLastName()); 18 ps.setInt(5, p.getYears()); 19 ps.addBatch(); 20 if (++count % batchSize == 0) ps.executeBatch(); 21 } 22 if (count % batchSize != 0) ps.executeBatch(); 23 conn.commit(); 24 } 25 } 26 } 27} The Surprising Result Strategy 100k persons (avg ms) Plain JDBC 3,905 Hibernate persist 4,048 JdbcTemplate 2,985 StatelessSession 2,650 Plain JDBC (3,905ms) is only 3% faster than Hibernate persist (4,048ms). The ORM overhead for batch inserts is negligible. Most of the time is spent in JDBC driver wire protocol and SQL Server's INSERT execution, not in Hibernate's entity management.
JdbcTemplate is actually faster than plain JDBC because Spring's JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate() uses optimized batch parameter binding that the JDBC driver can optimize further.
With useBulkCopyForBatchInsert=true Strategy Normal bulkCopy=true Speedup Plain JDBC 3,905 1,516 2.6x JdbcTemplate 3,089 1,373 2.3x StatelessSession 2,650 1,075 2.5x Hibernate persist 4,048 2,144 1.9x With bulkCopy=true, all JDBC-based strategies converge to similar performance. The driver's bulk copy conversion is the dominant factor, not the Java-side abstraction.
Multi-Value INSERT and bulkCopy Don't Mix During testing, we discovered that multi-value INSERT (objectsPerInsert > 1) is incompatible with useBulkCopyForBatchInsert=true. When this driver flag is enabled, it rewrites PreparedStatement.addBatch() calls into Bulk Copy protocol — but it expects single-row INSERT statements with exactly (columns) parameters per batch entry. Multi-value INSERT SQL (VALUES (?,?,?),(?,?,?),(?,?,?)...) confuses the driver because it has (columns * N) parameters.
This means you must choose one or the other:
Multi-value INSERT (400 values/statement) — works only with bulkCopy=false useBulkCopyForBatchInsert=true — works only with single-row INSERT statements Both are excellent optimizations, but they cannot be combined.
Isolation, MERGE, Triggers & Async Snapshot isolation (READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT) RCSI changes READ_COMMITTED to use row versioning instead of shared locks for reads. It prevents reader-writer blocking at the cost of version store overhead:
Strategy RCSI OFF RCSI ON Delta Bulk API 1,211 720 40% faster JdbcTemplate 2,817 3,565 27% slower Surprise: RCSI dramatically helps Bulk API (fewer latches/lock contention on data pages) but hurts JdbcTemplate (row versioning writes to tempdb). Enable RCSI if you're bulk-loading with the Bulk Copy protocol and have concurrent readers.
MERGE vs plain INSERT MERGE INTO ... USING (VALUES) WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT is the canonical SQL upsert. How much does the upsert semantics cost?
Method 100k rows (avg ms) Plain INSERT 3,177 MERGE upsert 3,514 (+11%) The 11% overhead is the cost of the ON clause evaluation and the branching logic. For pure inserts, use INSERT. For true upserts (where some rows may already exist), MERGE is cleaner than a SELECT-then-INSERT/UPDATE pattern.
Warning: MERGE has known bugs with concurrent executions on SQL Server. Many SQL Server MVPs recommend INSERT ... ON EXISTING UPDATE or explicit IF EXISTS patterns in production code.
Trigger overhead A single AFTER INSERT trigger that writes one audit row per insertion:
1CREATE TRIGGER tr_person_trigger_insert ON person_trigger 2AFTER INSERT AS 3BEGIN 4 SET NOCOUNT ON; 5 INSERT INTO person_audit (person_id, action) 6 SELECT person_id, 'INSERT' FROM inserted; 7END Scenario 100k rows (avg ms) No trigger 3,261 With AFTER INSERT trigger 7,023 (2.2x slower) Triggers are expensive. Each INSERT batch now does double the work — one for the base table, one for the audit table. Consider:
Logging via application code instead of triggers (gives you batching and backpressure control) Change Data Capture (CDC) — SQL Server reads the transaction log async Temporal tables (built-in system-versioned history) Async producer-consumer pipeline The sync baseline does CPU work (generating data) and I/O work (inserting) sequentially. A producer-consumer pipeline overlaps them:
1BlockingQueue<List<Person>> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(4); 2// Producer: generates batches of 1000, puts to queue 3// Consumer: polls queue, inserts batch Pattern 100k rows (avg ms) Sync baseline (CPU then I/O) 3,816 Async producer-consumer 2,676 (30% faster) A single-producer, single-consumer pipeline is enough to overlap work. More consumers would help only if the DB can accept more concurrent writers (see Part 6).
In-Memory OLTP, BULK INSERT & Stored Procedures BULK INSERT (server-side file reader) The BULK INSERT T-SQL command reads a flat file directly from the server's filesystem, bypassing the normal INSERT codepath entirely:
1BULK INSERT person FROM 'C:/ProgramData/bulk_data.txt' 2WITH (FORMAT = 'CSV', FIELDTERMINATOR = '0x09', ROWTERMINATOR = '0x0a', 3 BATCHSIZE = 1000, TABLOCK) Method 100k rows (avg ms) Ad-hoc INSERT batch 2,734 Single-threaded Bulk API 492 BULK INSERT (T-SQL) 637 BULK INSERT nearly matches the fastest single-threaded Java path. It's the ultimate pattern for server-local file imports — ETL/data warehousing scenarios where data lives on the SQL Server machine. The file must be readable by the SQL Server service account.
In-Memory OLTP Tables (MEMORY_OPTIMIZED = ON) In-Memory OLTP tables live entirely in RAM with lock-free, latch-free access. SQL Server 2016 SP1+ makes them available in all editions, including Express.
1CREATE TABLE person_memopt ( 2 person_id INT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY NONCLUSTERED, 3 user_name NVARCHAR(30), first_name NVARCHAR(10), 4 last_name NVARCHAR(15), years INT 5) WITH (MEMORY_OPTIMIZED = ON, DURABILITY = SCHEMA_AND_DATA); Scenario 100k rows (avg ms) Disk-based ad-hoc INSERT 2,734 In-Memory OLTP (interpreted T-SQL batch) 2,726 Surprise: essentially no benefit for batch inserts from Java. In-Memory tables excel at high-concurrency OLTP (many threads, many small operations) by eliminating latches. Our workload — one connection, batch of 1,000 rows — isn't lock-constrained; the bottleneck is the network and batch processing overhead, which both tables share.
Natively Compiled Stored Procedures Native compilation turns a stored proc into C code at creation time:
1CREATE PROCEDURE usp_InsertPerson_Native (...) 2WITH NATIVE_COMPILATION, SCHEMABINDING 3AS BEGIN ATOMIC WITH (TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL = SNAPSHOT, LANGUAGE = N'us_english') 4 INSERT INTO dbo.person_memopt (...) VALUES (...); 5END Scenario 100k rows (avg ms) In-Memory interpreted batch 2,726 Native proc called per-row via addBatch 58,542 (21x SLOWER) Native procs are a trap for Java clients. The native code itself is lightning fast, but you must call it per row (EXEC usp_... ?, ?, ?, ?, ?). The JDBC driver doesn't send 100,000 EXEC calls efficiently; each becomes its own RPC. The lesson: native procs win in C#/.NET memory-table batch APIs, not in Java JDBC.
Stored Procedures (interpreted) vs Ad-hoc Pattern 100k rows (avg ms) Ad-hoc INSERT (direct) 2,734 Stored procedure (EXEC usp_...) 4,807 (76% slower) A per-row stored procedure call is 76% slower than batched direct INSERT, for the same reason as native procs: each EXEC becomes a server-side command execution with its own parameter parsing and query plan lookup. Use procs for complex business logic, not for simple inserts.
Check Constraints Scenario 100k rows (avg ms) Check constraints enabled 2,954 Check constraints disabled 2,909 Simple check constraints are essentially free. For LEN(x) > 0 and range checks, the overhead is negligible. Only disable constraints with ALTER TABLE NOCHECK CONSTRAINT ALL for complex multi-table FK checks on large bulk loads — simple column constraints are fine to leave on.
Query Plans, Latency & INSERT…SELECT OPTION(RECOMPILE) — catastrophic for batches Adding OPTION (RECOMPILE) to an INSERT forces SQL Server to recompile the query plan for every execution:
Scenario 100k rows (avg ms) Normal (plan cached across batches) 2,772 OPTION (RECOMPILE) 145,097 (52x SLOWER!) Never use OPTION (RECOMPILE) with batched INSERTs. Each row-group recompiles the plan, turning a 3-second operation into a 2.4-minute one. The hint is for one-off queries with wildly varying parameters, not high-volume batched workloads.
Network latency simulation Simulated by inserting Thread.sleep(ms) after each executeBatch():
Added latency 100k rows (avg ms) 0 ms (local) 2,759 1 ms per batch (×100 batches) 2,948 (+7%) 5 ms per batch (×100 batches) 4,370 (+58%) Each 1 ms of round-trip latency per batch adds ~1 ms × (number of batches) overhead. On a production WAN link with 20-50 ms RTT, 100k inserts in 1000-row batches would spend 2-5 seconds in network overhead alone. Larger batches amortize the latency — the single-threaded Bulk Copy protocol (~1 batch total) is nearly immune.
INSERT … SELECT (data already in the server) If your source data is already on the SQL Server (another table, a staging table, etc.), the fastest possible path is INSERT INTO target SELECT ... FROM source — no client round-trips at all:
Pattern 100k rows (avg ms) INSERT … SELECT (plain) 319 INSERT … SELECT … ORDER BY 447 (+40% for sort) Parallel Bulk API 4t 330 INSERT…SELECT is the fastest method we've benchmarked, matching Parallel Bulk API. It's the right choice for ETL pipelines, materialized view refreshes, and in-database transformations. The 40% ORDER BY penalty is the cost of the sort — if your clustered key already matches the ORDER BY, the sort disappears.
SQLServerBulkCopy option tuning Fine-tuning SQLServerBulkCopyOptions:
Option 100k rows (avg ms) Default (batch 1000) 765 batchSize = 5000 535 (30% faster) + checkConstraints = true 619 + tableLock = true 662 Bigger batch = fewer round-trips — 5000 beats 1000 by 30%. checkConstraints = true adds ~15% but validates FKs/CHECKs that are normally skipped during bulk load (the default is false, meaning the loaded data is marked as untrusted). tableLock = true acquires a bulk-update lock on the table — helpful when there are concurrent writers, but prevents reader access during the load. SNAPSHOT Isolation Under Write Contention Part 8 already covered RCSI which turns READ COMMITTED into snapshot-based. Here we test full SNAPSHOT isolation (ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION ON + SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT) under concurrent reads during a bulk insert.
Scenario Insert time Reader throughput SNAPSHOT single writer (no readers) 2,997 ms — READ_COMMITTED + 4 concurrent readers 2,964 ms ~8 reads total (blocked by writer locks) SNAPSHOT + 2 concurrent readers 4,638 ms (+55%) ~430 reads per run SNAPSHOT + 4 concurrent readers 6,259 ms (+109%) ~1,100 reads per run The trade-off is stark:
With READ_COMMITTED: writes stay fast but readers get almost nothing (~8 reads vs 1,100). With SNAPSHOT: readers aren't blocked (135x more throughput), but writes are 2x slower due to version-store overhead. Pick based on your workload: if readers must stay responsive during bulk loads, pay the SNAPSHOT cost. If the load window is dedicated (no readers care), RC is fine.
Partition SWITCH with Indexes Earlier we saw SWITCH PARTITION is a metadata-only operation. But the load into staging still has to maintain any indexes that match the target. How much does pre-indexing the staging table cost?
Target indexes 100k rows total (load + SWITCH) 0 non-clustered 2,952 ms 1 non-clustered 4,205 ms (+42%) 3 non-clustered 6,369 ms (+116%) Just like non-partitioned tables, index maintenance is the dominant cost. If possible: load into a heap staging table, then build the matching indexes on it right before the SWITCH — this is usually faster than maintaining indexes during the load.
Semi-Structured Indexes: XML vs JSON Part 7 showed XML columns cost 2.3x more than JSON for storage. What about indexes on those columns?
XML Primary Index 1CREATE PRIMARY XML INDEX PXML_person_xml_idx_data ON person_xml_idx(data); The XML primary index is a shredded node table — one row per XML node per document. For 100k documents with ~5 nodes each, that's 500,000 node-table rows maintained on every insert.
XML column 100k rows (avg ms) No XML index 8,339 + PRIMARY XML INDEX 38,265 (4.6x SLOWER!) JSON Computed-Column Index JSON doesn't have a native index type in SQL Server. The idiomatic pattern is:
1ALTER TABLE person_json_idx 2 ADD years_from_json AS JSON_VALUE(data, '$.years'); 3CREATE INDEX IX_person_json_idx_years ON person_json_idx(years_from_json); JSON column 100k rows (avg ms) No JSON index 5,774 + computed-column INDEX 8,493 (+47%) JSON indexes are 10x cheaper than XML indexes (+47% vs +359%) because JSON uses a scalar computed column — just one indexed value per row — while the XML index shreds the entire document.
Takeaway: if you need to query JSON/XML by a specific field, use the JSON computed-column pattern. XML primary indexes are only worth it for complex XQuery/XPath workloads.
tempdb Spill (Memory Grant Starvation) What happens when SQL Server's memory grant for a sort is insufficient and it has to spill to tempdb? We force a tiny grant with OPTION (MIN_GRANT_PERCENT = 0, MAX_GRANT_PERCENT = 0.001):
INSERT…SELECT + ORDER BY 100k rows (avg ms) Normal grant (in-memory sort) 326 Tiny grant (tempdb spill) 657 (2x slower) Spilling to tempdb is cheaper than you'd expect. Only 2x slower — SQL Server handles spills gracefully with multi-pass merge sorts. The right lesson: don't panic if you see occasional spills in a slow query report; focus on queries that spill gigabytes, not kilobytes.
Final Rankings: All Strategies Combined Across the ~110 configurations we tested, here are the headline numbers. All ran on SQL Server 2025 Express (local), Java 17 + Spring Boot 3.3, 100k rows unless noted.
Fastest paths Rank Strategy 100k avg ms Covered in Notes 1 INSERT … SELECT (same DB) 319 Part 8 Server-side copy — no round-trips 2 Parallel Bulk API 4t 330 Part 6 Fastest Java client-driven path 3 Multi-value 400 + 8 threads 368 Parts 3+6 No bulkCopy flag needed 4 Multi-value 400 + 4 threads 426 Parts 3+6 5 Parallel Bulk API 8t 434 Part 6 Diminishing returns past 4 threads 6 INSERT…SELECT ORDER BY 447 Part 8 +40% for the sort 7 Bulk API (single thread) 492 Part 2 Fastest single-thread 8 SQLServerBulkCopy batch=5000 535 Part 8 Bigger batch wins 9 Parallel Bulk API 4t + bulkCopy 603 Parts 6+4 bulkCopy on bulk is redundant 10 Parallel JdbcTemplate 16t 608 Part 6 11 BULK INSERT (T-SQL from file) 637 Part 8 Server-side file reader 12 SQLServerBulkCopy +TABLOCK 662 Part 8 13 Parallel JdbcTemplate 4t + bulkCopy 731 Parts 6+4 14 TVP (batch=5000) 818 Part 8 Best portable single-thread Mid-tier Rank Strategy 100k avg ms 15 Multi-value 400 single thread 1,058 16 StatelessSession + bulkCopy 1,075 17 JdbcTemplate + bulkCopy 1,373 18 Plain JDBC + bulkCopy 1,516 19 Clustered + TABLOCK 2,185 20 Hibernate + bulkCopy 2,144 21 JDBC PreparedStatement 2,423 22 StatelessSession 2,650 23 In-Memory OLTP (interpreted batch) 2,726 24 JdbcTemplate 2,985 Slow & anti-patterns Rank Strategy 100k avg ms Why 25 SWITCH + 3 indexes 6,369 Index maintenance in staging 26 Columnstore + batch 1000 8,402 Delta store overhead 27 AFTER INSERT trigger 7,023 Secondary insert per row 28 XML column (no index) 8,339 Native XML tree parsing 29 XML + PRIMARY XML INDEX 38,265 Shredded node table maintenance 30 Server-side encryption (3 cols) 15,952 AES per row 31 Native proc per-row EXEC 58,542 No batching with addBatch 32 OPTION (RECOMPILE) + batches 145,097 Plan rebuilt per execution 33 saveAll (original, Spring Data JPA) 27,794 SELECT per entity (merge) Headline: INSERT…SELECT (319 ms) is the fastest; OPTION (RECOMPILE) with batches is 455x slower than the best.
Key Takeaways from the Series Parallel Bulk API is the overall winner (330ms for 100k rows). The Bulk Copy API already uses an optimized protocol; splitting across threads adds connection-level parallelism.
Multi-value INSERT + parallel threads (368ms) is a close second and doesn't require useBulkCopyForBatchInsert or the Bulk Copy API — it works with any JDBC driver.
useBulkCopyForBatchInsert=true gives 2-2.5x speedup to single-row batch strategies. One connection string parameter is the easiest win. But it's incompatible with multi-value INSERT.
Hibernate's overhead is ~3% for batch inserts. The ORM is not the bottleneck; the network and database engine are.
Parallelism helps 2-7x depending on the strategy and thread count. 4 threads is the safe default; 8-16 helps JdbcTemplate more than Bulk API.
Indexes are the hidden cost — 5 non-clustered indexes make inserts 6-7x slower regardless of strategy. Drop and rebuild indexes for bulk loads.
TVPs are underrated — 3rd fastest single-thread strategy with a clean API, no parameter count limits, and works inside transactions.
Batch size sweet spot is 500-1000 for most strategies. Below 200, overhead dominates; above 1000, diminishing returns.
Multi-value objectsPerInsert sweet spot is 200 — beyond that, SQL parser overhead increases faster than network savings decrease.
Compression hurts inserts — ROW (+7%) and PAGE (+33%) compression add CPU overhead that outweighs I/O savings for writes. Save compression for read-heavy tables.
BCP (843ms) is slower than Java Bulk API (691ms) for in-memory data — file I/O is the bottleneck, not the protocol.
Concurrent readers slow inserts 2.5x — use TABLOCK for dedicated bulk-load windows to prevent reader contention.
Columnstore tables are 3.5x slower for OLTP-style inserts — the delta store overhead only pays off at analytical query time.
Auto-commit per row is 15x slower than batched transactions — never do it.
Isolation level and GC choice don't matter for INSERT-only workloads. Default READ_COMMITTED + default G1 are fine; tuning them is wasted effort.
Fill factor 100 is best for sequential IDs. Lower fill factors (70-80) only help with random-key inserts that cause page splits.
SWITCH PARTITION is the gold standard for zero-downtime bulk loads — load a staging heap, then atomically metadata-swap it into a partition (milliseconds, regardless of size).
RCSI (snapshot isolation) is a Bulk API accelerator. Enable it if you use Bulk API and have concurrent readers — 40% faster. But it slows JDBC batches 27% due to version store overhead; don't enable it blindly.
MERGE costs 11% over plain INSERT for upsert semantics. Use INSERT for pure appends.
AFTER INSERT triggers are 2.2x slower. Prefer application logging, CDC, or temporal tables for audit trails.
Async producer-consumer is 30% faster than sync by overlapping CPU and I/O work. Even one producer + one consumer is enough.
Random GUID clustered keys cost 19% minimum on empty tables, far more on populated ones (page splits). Use NEWSEQUENTIALID() or an ordered GUID (UUIDv7/ULID) if you must use GUIDs.
Change Tracking is expensive (62% overhead). Enable only if a downstream consumer actually reads the change feed. Full CDC (Enterprise only) is even more expensive.
Temporal tables are cheap for audit (+31%) — far better than AFTER INSERT triggers (+120%). The right answer for most point-in-time history requirements.
Filtered indexes are 60% cheaper than full indexes on the same column. If your queries only need a subset of rows, index only that subset.
INCLUDE is 30% cheaper than composite — storing columns only at the leaf level is cheaper than making them part of the sort key.
Computed columns are essentially free on insert (persisted +0%, non-persisted +0%). Use them for derived values; they're cleaner than app-side computations and support indexing.
Delayed Durability can make bulk inserts SLOWER (+49%) — it's a per-transaction optimization for many small commits, not for single large transactions.
Trace flag 610 doesn't help regular INSERTs — only BULK INSERT, BCP, and INSERT ... SELECT benefit. The JDBC Bulk Copy API already handles this transparently.
XML columns are 2.3x slower than JSON (NVARCHAR+ISJSON) for the same payload. Use JSON unless you specifically need XQuery/XPath.
Sparse columns are 14% SLOWER when columns are populated. Only use SPARSE when the column is >95% NULL in real data — otherwise it's a lose-lose.
AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS = OFF makes inserts 50% slower, not faster — the optimizer needs stats even for simple INSERTs. Always leave it ON.
Server-side encryption (ENCRYPTBYPASSPHRASE) is 4x slower for 3 encrypted columns. Prefer Always Encrypted (client-side) or TDE (page-level) for most PII protection use cases.
BULK INSERT from file (637ms) rivals Java Bulk API when data already lives on the SQL Server machine. The server-side bulk reader is as fast as the Java client-side protocol.
In-Memory OLTP tables offer no benefit for batched Java inserts. They shine for high-concurrency OLTP; our one-thread batch workload isn't lock-constrained.
Natively compiled procedures are a trap for Java clients — 21x slower when called per-row via addBatch. They're designed for the memory-table API in .NET/C#, not JDBC.
Stored procedures (interpreted) are 76% slower than direct INSERT batches. Use procs for complex logic, not simple row inserts.
Check constraints are free for simple column validations. Only disable them for complex FK validation on huge bulk loads.
RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS costs +34%. Suppress it in your ORM/JDBC code if you don't need the generated IDs back on insert.
App-generated IDs beat IDENTITY and SEQUENCE by 12-31%. Prefer ULID/Snowflake/pre-fetched sequence batches to server-side ID generation for the fastest batched inserts.
Trusted FKs cost +21% — disable before bulk loads, then WITH CHECK CHECK CONSTRAINT to re-validate (faster than per-row checking).
Abort-on-error batches are 7.5x faster than per-row insert retry, but you lose up to 999 good rows per bad row. Pick based on data cleanliness and tolerance for row loss.
OPTION (RECOMPILE) is a batch-insert killer — 52x slower. Never use it with batched workloads.
Network latency amortizes with larger batches. 5 ms RTT per batch costs 500 ms over 100 batches but 0 ms if you make it a single Bulk Copy call.
INSERT … SELECT (server-side) is the fastest path at 319 ms — matches Parallel Bulk API. If your data is already on the server, don't round-trip through the client.
Bigger SQLServerBulkCopyOptions.batchSize wins — 5000 beats 1000 by 30%. Default is a conservative starting point, not the optimum.
SNAPSHOT isolation lets concurrent readers do 135x more work during a bulk load (1,100 reads vs 8), but writes 2x slower. Pick based on whether readers need to stay responsive.
SWITCH PARTITION's load phase scales linearly with index count — just like non-partitioned tables. Load into a heap, then add matching indexes right before the SWITCH.
XML primary indexes are 4.6x more expensive than JSON computed-column indexes (+359% vs +47%). Use JSON unless you specifically need XQuery/XPath.
tempdb spills are cheap — only 2x slower than in-memory sort. Don't panic over small spills.
What to actually do If you take only one thing from the whole series: batch your inserts and don't fight the protocol. A proper batch strategy puts you within 10x of the fastest possible path on day one. From there:
Data already on the server → INSERT…SELECT (319 ms). Pushing from Java → Parallel Bulk API with 4 threads (330 ms), or multi-value INSERT with 200 rows per statement if you need portability. Stuck on Hibernate → implement Persistable<T> and set useBulkCopyForBatchInsert=true — 1,075 ms is as fast as you'll get without leaving the ORM. Avoid these → OPTION (RECOMPILE) with batches (145 s), AFTER INSERT triggers (2.2x), server-side encryption on every column (4x), per-row stored proc EXEC (76% penalty). The full benchmark code — 18 test classes, 4,222 runs, 17 charts — is in the blog-examples repository. Clone it, point it at your own SQL Server, and the numbers will shift — but the rankings will almost certainly hold.
Test yourself What is the absolute fastest insert path measured in the series?
Parallel Bulk API, 4 threads INSERT...SELECT on the same server Table-Valued Parameters Natively compiled stored procedure Check answer INSERT...SELECT (data already on the server) finished in 319 ms, fastest overall. Parallel Bulk API at 330 ms is the fastest path when pushing from Java.
Why is OPTION(RECOMPILE) dangerous with batched inserts?
It disables batching It forces a plan recompile per batch, making it about 52x slower It locks the whole table It silently drops rows Check answer OPTION(RECOMPILE) recompiles the plan for every batch: 145 s vs 2.8 s, about 52x slower. Never combine it with batched inserts.

Ten questions covering the biggest findings from the Fastest MS SQL Inserts series. All answers come from measured benchmarks on SQL Server 2025 (Java 17, Spring Boot 3.3, 100,000 rows).
Click a question to reveal the answer and the post it came from. No tracking, no scoring — just honest "did I remember this?"
1. Which single-strategy approach inserts 100,000 rows into SQL Server the fastest from Java? Reveal answer Parallel Bulk API with 4 threads — 330 ms.
The Bulk Copy protocol already minimises per-row overhead, and splitting the data across 4 connections saturates SQL Server's I/O without adding meaningful contention. Eight threads shaves another ~100 ms; sixteen is noise.
Source: Part 6 — Parallel Threads 2. There's an even faster path than that one. What is it, and when can you use it? Reveal answer INSERT INTO target SELECT ... FROM source — 319 ms.
If your data is already on the SQL Server (another table, a staging table, a view), server-side INSERT…SELECT beats every client-driven approach because there are no network round-trips. Only usable when the source lives in the database — not for data you're pushing from an application.
Source: Part 8 — Final Ranking 3. True or false: adding OPTION (RECOMPILE) to batched INSERTs usually improves performance. Reveal answer False — it's 52× slower.
Normal batched inserts take 2,772 ms; with OPTION (RECOMPILE) the same workload takes 145,097 ms — 2 minutes 25 seconds. Each batch forces a new plan compile, destroying plan-cache reuse. The hint is for one-off queries with wildly varying parameters, not for high-volume batched workloads.
Source: Part 8 — Query Plans & Latency 4. You turn OFF AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS on a database because the stats maintenance keeps interrupting your bulk load. What happens to insert throughput? Reveal answer It gets 50% SLOWER, not faster.
Default (ON) averaged 2,966 ms; OFF averaged 4,474 ms. The optimizer uses statistics to choose INSERT plans — access paths, batch sizes, memory grants — even for simple single-table inserts with no WHERE clause. Starving it of fresh stats forces worse plans.
Source: Part 7 — Table Design 5. Spring Data's default JpaRepository.saveAll() was taking 27.8 seconds for 100k entities. What one change (no library swap) makes it 8× faster? Reveal answer Implement Persistable<ID> on the entity, with isNew() = true.
saveAll is slow because Spring Data calls EntityManager.merge() on every entity, which triggers a SELECT before each INSERT to check for an existing row. When isNew() returns true, Spring Data uses persist() directly — no SELECTs. Original: 27,794 ms. With Persistable: 3,426 ms.
Source: Part 5 — Hibernate Tuning 6. There's one connection-string flag that gives a 2–2.5× speedup to Hibernate, JdbcTemplate, StatelessSession and plain JDBC batched inserts. Which one, and what's its catch? Reveal answer useBulkCopyForBatchInsert=true in the JDBC URL.
The Microsoft SQL JDBC driver silently rewrites PreparedStatement.addBatch() calls into the Bulk Copy protocol. Catch: incompatible with multi-value INSERT (VALUES (?,?,?),(?,?,?)... style) — the driver rewrites single-row INSERTs only. Pick either multi-value or bulkCopy=true, not both.
Source: Part 4 — Bulk Copy Flag, Part 5, Part 8 7. How much does adding 5 non-clustered indexes to a table slow down inserts, and does the choice of client-side strategy still matter? Reveal answer Inserts are 6-11× slower, and strategy choice stops mattering.
Indexes Bulk API JdbcTemplate Hibernate 0 784 ms 4,572 ms 3,209 ms 5 5,290 ms (+575%) 10,330 ms (+126%) 8,564 ms (+167%) With many indexes, index maintenance dominates and strategies converge. The right fix is drop indexes before the load, rebuild after.
Source: Part 7 — Index Impact 8. You're on an older SQL Server driver without SQLServerBulkCopy. What's the fastest portable alternative? Reveal answer Table-Valued Parameters (TVPs) — 818 ms at batch size 5,000.
TVPs let you send an entire table of data as a single parameter — one network round-trip per batch instead of N. Works with any JDBC driver that supports java.sql.CallableStatement. TVPs beat every pure-JDBC strategy except the proprietary Bulk Copy API.
Source: Part 8 — TVP, JDBC, Final Ranking 9. Native-compiled stored procedures feel like the fastest possible path. Why are they a trap when called from Java? Reveal answer They're 21× slower when called via addBatch — 58,542 ms vs 2,726 ms baseline.
Native procs are designed for the C#/.NET memory-table API, which can batch rows into one call. From Java, each EXEC usp_... ?, ?, ?, ?, ? becomes its own RPC — the compilation speed-up is swamped by per-row network round-trips. Use native procs only if you can call them via a bulk memory-table API, not per-row.
Source: Part 8 — In-Memory OLTP & Procs 10. True or false: ROW and PAGE compression on the destination table make inserts faster because less data is written to disk. Reveal answer False — ROW adds 7% overhead, PAGE adds 33%.
Compression is a read optimization (smaller pages → faster scans and cache hits). On write, every row must be compressed on the way in, which costs CPU; for narrow rows like person, the compression ratio is too small to earn back the CPU time. For your tables, if inserts are the bottleneck, don't enable compression — leave it for read-heavy tables with wide rows.
Source: Part 7 — Table Design & Logging How did you do?
10/10 — you've probably implemented this stuff already. Nice. 7-9/10 — solid. Skim the ones you missed to lock them in. Under 7/10 — start with Part 1 and work forward. Each part builds on the last. Found a question that should be on this list? Open an issue or tweet at me.
